central_question: What will the global EV industry trajectory look like from 2026 to 2035, including adoption rates, regional bifurcation, technology evolution, and policy frameworks?

situation_brief.current_situation: The global EV industry stands at an inflection point in mid-2026: approximately 20 million EVs were sold globally in 2025 (25% market share), but the market has bifurcated sharply by region. China captured 63% of 2025 global EV sales and reached 53% domestic penetration, while the US market collapsed from a 10.6% Q3 2025 peak to 5.8% by Q2 2026 following expiration of the $7,500 federal tax credit on September 30, 2025. The European Commission's December 16, 2025 proposal softened the 2035 ICE ban to a 90% CO₂ reduction, representing the most significant policy reversal in the industry's history. The Iran war (started February 28, 2026) and Strait of Hormuz disruptions created oil-price volatility that paradoxically boosted EV consumer interest while increasing battery raw material costs.
situation_brief.context: The EV transition reached 25% global market share in 2025 through a combination of Chinese industrial policy (dual-credit system, NEV mandate from 2018), European regulatory push (2023 100% CO₂ reduction by 2035), and US Inflation Reduction Act incentives ($7,500 federal credit). The June 2025 lithium price trough (~$9,000/tonne) and continued LFP cost-down brought battery pack prices to $108/kWh. However, the Trump administration's 'One Big Beautiful Bill' (signed July 4, 2025) terminated EV credits effective September 30, 2025, triggering a US demand cliff (−36% YoY Q4 2025). Simultaneously, German automotive industry lobbying and Chinese competitive pressure drove the EU's December 2025 retreat from the original 2035 ICE ban.
situation_brief.dynamics: Three forces are in tension: (1) Policy stability versus reversal, with the EU 90% proposal facing Parliament resistance and trilogue negotiations through 2026-2027, while 17 US states plus DC (~40% of US market) maintain ACC II ZEV mandates despite federal preemption attempts. (2) Cost reduction versus raw material volatility, with battery pack prices falling despite lithium carbonate rebounding 170% from June 2025 lows to exceed $25,000/tonne by June 2026. (3) Chinese export expansion versus Western protectionism, with BYD's June 2026 overseas sales up 94.73% year-over-year confronting 100% US Section 301 tariffs and EU anti-subsidy duties. Western OEMs recorded massive EV-related charges: Ford $19.5 billion cumulative losses, GM $7.2 billion Q4 2025 special charges, Stellantis €22 billion. Tesla's Q2 2026 deliveries of 480,126 units (+25% YoY, +18% consensus beat) signal selective recovery.
